title: Control Plane Adapter Role Matrix and Routing Guidelines
content:
Purpose / quick summary:
- Working sketch to define clear role boundaries between API gateway, orchestration (control-plane core), runtime adapters (region-specific runtime proxies), and policy/routing engines.
- Target audience: platform eng leads, runtime owners, SRE, solutions eng.
- Goal: reduce ambiguity that causes cross-team outages and unblock a low-friction multi-region routing rollout.

Context and motivation:
- We've observed gaps when we try to do cross-region failovers or model variant rollouts: who owns the route transformation, where is model affinity enforced, and who owns the fallback policy?
- Current symptoms: ad-hoc routing in gateway config, per-team adapter features, and orchestration having hidden assumptions about runtime capabilities.

High-level roles (short declarative):
- API Gateway (edge-gateway): terminate client TLS, basic auth/rate-limit, header normalization, and responsibility for request ingress shaping only. DOES NOT inject model-specific routing logic or region fallback decisioning beyond configured static weights.
- Control-Plane Orchestrator (planner): maintains global desired state (model versions, deployment sets, rollout policies, weights), exposes canonical routing directives (policy objects) via a typed control API consumed by the routing engine. Responsible for generating canary/A-B definitions, but not for low-latency per-request evaluation.
- Routing Policy Engine (RPE): a lightweight, highly-available service colocated near gateway or as a sidecar that evaluates per-request routing at millisecond latency using the orchestrator policy objects + local telemetry. Responsible for region selection, model affinity, and fallback decisioning when runtime signals are degraded.
- Runtime Adapters (region runtime proxies): region- and infra-aware translators that map canonical model endpoints to local runtime endpoints, manage connection pooling/KV-cache hints, and implement capacity-aware throttles. Owns the contract to the serving runtime (batching, quantization profile selection, kernel hints) and reports health/metrics to SRE.
- Local Config Store / Feature Flags: used for transient overrides (eg, PB/experiments) but not for long-lived routing policies.

Proposed ownership split (who-does-what):
- Gateway team: TLS, rate-limit, identity, schema validation, and fast-path header rewrites. Gateway consumes endpoint hostnames from RPE but does not do model selection logic.
- Orchestration team: author and own policy model (Policy CRD), rollout orchestration orchestration service, author canary rules, publish to central policy-store; own integrations with CI/CD for canary automation.
- RPE team (new-ish): implement deterministic eval service, maintain local cache of policies, expose thin API to gateway and adapters, own per-request routing logs (for audits).
- Runtime adapter teams (per-region): implement adapter shim, own adapter health checks, and ensure adapter implements the canonical mapping contract to runtime.
- SRE/platform: own alerting/SLIs across these components; own escalation runbooks for cross-component failovers.

Routing policy examples (canonical objects):
- Policy object: {name, model_family, allowed_regions[], priority, fallback_strategy, traffic_split}, stored in orchestration. (NOTE: JSON here for readability, canonical proto will be defined in follow-up)
- Canary: orchestration creates a CanaryPolicy referencing model_version_id + traffic_split 5% -> RPE will honor and route accordingly.
- Degraded runtime fallback: fallback_strategy = [local-fallback, cross-region-sync, degraded-model]. RPE must attempt local-fallback first; if latency/error exceeds threshold, switch per-request.

Latency-sensitive flows and placement guidance:
- RPE must be colocated with gateway in the same AZ/edge location when low tail latency is required for hosted API customers.
- For Dedicated/private deployments, RPE can be embedded as a sidecar inside customer control plane or as an on-prem lightweight service.
- Runtime adapters should be deployed per-region and expose capacity signals (available_gpus, pending_queue_ms, kv-cache-hit-rate).

Failure modes and graceful degradation patterns:
- Orchestration unreachable: RPE must continue to serve from cached policies with TTL; establish conservative TTL policy (eg 1 minute for dynamic rollout, 10 minutes for stable policies).
- RPE unhealthy: gateway falls back to static host lists provided by orchestration last-known-state; adapt with stricter rate-limits.
- Adapter partial outage: adapter returns 503 for model_family -> RPE records and switches traffic to next best region/model.
- Regional network partition: RPE must prefer same-region runtime adapters with strong affinity; orchestrator-level override used only after human review for partial partitions.

Implementation constraints / contracts (practical):
- All route decisions must be reproducible from: orchestration policy object + adapter-reported capacity snapshot + request attributes (region_hint, customer_tier, model_pref).
- Adapters MUST implement health and capacity endpoints: /health, /metrics, /capacity-summary (simple JSON).
- RPE API: evaluateRoute(requestContext) -> {target_runtime_endpoint, rationale_code, policy_version}. Keep small surface area.
- Policy versioning is REQUIRED; RPEs must report policy_version on routed requests for tracing.

Data and observability requirements:
- Per-request routing log with: request_id, policy_version, chosen_endpoint, latency_ms, fallback_reason (if any), adapter_capacity_snapshot. Store sampling at 100% for errors and 1% for success.
- Dashboards: cross-region routing heatmap, policy rollout progress, adapter capacity headroom trends.

Multi-region specifics and consistency tradeoffs:
- Eventual consistency is acceptable for policy publication (push model + local cache), but critical docs (policy_version bumps for emergency rollouts) should support a strong push path (publish-and-wait acknowledgement from all active RPEs).
- Prefer local decisioning for per-request latency; avoid orchestration sync in request path.
- Cross-region memory: KV-cache prefixes are local to runtime; adapters must not assume global cache coherence.

Open questions / design tradeoffs to resolve:
- Where does authz of fine-grained policy edits live? (Orchestration-admin vs gateway-admin) Current leaning: only orchestration-admin can update policy objects; gateway-admins can apply temporary overrides but must be audited.
- Is the RPE a separate service or a library (embedded in gateway)? Tradeoffs: deployment simplicity vs team boundaries. Proposal: reference implementation as a library with a service wrapper to allow both modes.
- How aggressive should TTLs be for cached policies during global rollouts? Default: short for dynamic rollouts (30–60s), longer for stable releases (10m).
- How granular should adapter capacity signals be? Minimal viable: available_slots, avg_queue_ms, gpu_mem_pct.

Quick roll plan (next steps / action items):
- Priya: draft the canonical Policy proto and a minimal example (due 2026-03-05).
- Miguel: prototype an RPE eval API stub and benchmark p99 overhead when colocated with Envoy (due 2026-03-12).
- Evan: adapter health + capacity schema proposal and sample implementation for us-west-2 (due 2026-03-15).
- Aisha (owner): schedule cross-team sync (platform + gateway + runtime) week of 2026-02-27; create follow-up RFC.

Notes / shorthand log:
- 2025-11-20: observed 2 incidents where gateway-level weighted routing caused model split violations during canary -> root cause: gateway had local config unaware of orchestration policy_version.
- 2025-12-08: chat #platform: RPE idea seeded by Evan; consensus to explore library-first approach.

References / links:
- Confluence: CONF-PLAT-8472 (routing policy design anchor)
- Jira: JIRA-PLAT-1293 (adapter health telemetry work)
- Prototype code: github.com/redwood-inference/route-prototypes/pull/58

Appendix (short examples / snippets):
- Example fallback sequence (pseudocode):
  1) request -> gateway -> RPE.evaluate(request)
  2) RPE checks local policy + adapter capacity -> choose endpoint
  3) if endpoint error or high latency -> mark adapter degraded, consult fallback list -> switch to cross-region endpoint with lower affinity
  4) emit routing_log + increment policy_fallback_metric

Unresolved: policy CRD shape (proto vs JSON schema). Will converge in policy proto draft.

-- end of sketch --

Comments welcome — this is intentionally lightweight; want to capture practical constraints and clear ownership boundaries before drafting a formal RFC.
